content: Central obesity, also referred to as apple-shaped or masculine obesity, is characterized by the accumulation of body fat predominantly around the abdomen and upper body. This condition is closely associated with the presence of visceral fat, which is fat stored within the abdominal cavity and surrounding internal organs. Central obesity is frequently observed in individuals with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and metabolic syndrome. It is linked to a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Additionally, central obesity can be a clinical feature of lipodystrophies, which are a group of disorders that may be inherited or caused by secondary factors, such as the use of protease inhibitors—medications commonly used in the treatment of AIDS. Despite the colloquial terms beer belly, beer gut, or pot belly, there is limited scientific evidence to support the notion that beer consumption specifically predisposes individuals to abdominal obesity. Certain medications, such as dolutegravir and zidovudine, have been identified as potential contributors to central obesity as a side effect. The diagnosis of central obesity is typically made by measuring the waist-to-hip ratio. A ratio exceeding 1.0 in men or 0.9 in women is indicative of central obesity. The primary approach to managing central obesity involves weight loss, particularly when the condition is considered cosmetically undesirable or when it increases the risk of associated diseases. Adjunctive pharmacological treatments may include the use of orlistat or sibutramine to aid in weight reduction. In patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, physicians may prefer prescribing metformin or thiazolidinediones (such as rosiglitazone or pioglitazone) as antidiabetic agents, rather than sulfonylurea derivatives, due to their potential benefits in addressing insulin resistance and fat distribution. The term love handles is a colloquial expression used to describe the accumulation of fat around the midsection, particularly on the sides over the external oblique muscles of the abdomen. The name love handles may stem from their association with physical affection, as they provide a soft area to rest one's hand or hold onto during intimate moments. Love handles are more commonly observed in men than in women, as men tend to store fat in the abdominal region, whereas women are more likely to accumulate fat around the hips and thighs. These fat deposits often become more prominent with age, particularly as individuals approach middle age and experience a decline in physical activity levels. Both men and women may develop negative body image concerns related to the presence of love handles. While numerous products claim to target and eliminate love handles, it is widely accepted that spot reduction is not feasible. The most effective strategy for reducing love handles involves overall fat loss through increased physical activity, such as cardiovascular exercise and strength training, combined with a reduction in caloric intake. Love handles are also colloquially referred to as a spare tire, due to the resemblance of the fat deposits to the shape of an inflated tire encircling the midsection.
